items.explanation: Gilded Age parties were intensely competitive but internally fractured: Republicans and Democrats each contained pro- and anti-tariff wings, and the gold-versus-silver currency fight cut across both parties. That made it nearly impossible to assemble a majority for big national reforms, while voters still turned out in droves out of party loyalty, Civil War-era allegiances, and patronage ties. High participation and legislative stalemate were two sides of the same party system.
items.fact_source: Gilded Age electoral politics - high voter turnout, closely balanced parties, internal party divisions over tariffs and the gold/silver currency question; limited federal domestic reform legislation.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. This projects modern expectations onto the past. Gilded Age voters mobilized around party identity, Civil War loyalties, and patronage -- not around a belief that Washington should manage the economy.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Close elections reflected two evenly matched party machines, not voters dividing sharply over issues; competitiveness alone does not show issue-driven voting.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The tariff mattered, but one issue cannot explain both mass turnout and legislative stalemate -- the parties were internally divided on the tariff itself.
option_explanations.D: Right. Cross-cutting internal divisions over tariffs, currency, and patronage kept either party from uniting behind a national reform program, even as party loyalty and identity drove record turnout.

options: (A) Voters turned out in large numbers because they expected the federal government to solve economic problems directly, as modern voters do
(B) Because elections were so close, the parties must have differed sharply on major issues, which is what drove voters to the polls
(C) Voters chose parties based on the tariff alone, so tariff policy explains both the high turnout and the lack of other reforms
(D) Both parties were divided internally over tariffs, currency, and patronage, so neither could unite behind national reforms.
items.stem: During the Gilded Age, presidential elections were fiercely contested, voter turnout often exceeded 75 percent, and the two parties were nearly evenly matched -- yet the federal government enacted few major domestic reforms. Which of the following best explains this apparent contradiction?

items.explanation: The Sherman Act was written to curb trusts, but in the 1890s prosecutors and courts turned it against unions -- most famously in the 1894 Pullman strike, when a federal court used the Act to enjoin Eugene Debs and the American Railway Union. The first major successful use against an actual corporate combination did not come until the Northern Securities case in 1904. Passing the law, the mergers that followed it, and its later reputation do not show it achieved its purpose in the 1890s.
items.fact_source: Sherman Antitrust Act (1890); federal injunction against the Pullman strike, upheld in In re Debs (1895); Northern Securities Co. v. United States (1904); the 1895-1904 merger movement (including U.S. Steel, 1901).

option_explanations.A: Wrong. This confuses passing a law with achieving its goal. Congress can pass an antitrust law while enforcement goes in a different direction -- the statute's text is not evidence of its effects.
option_explanations.B: Right. The Act's earliest high-profile courtroom uses, including the 1894 Pullman strike injunction upheld in In re Debs (1895), were aimed at organized labor rather than at the corporate combinations the law was written to restrain.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. That the merger wave followed the Act does not prove the Act caused it; sequence is not causation, and consolidation grew for other reasons.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. That modern antitrust law descends from the Sherman Act shows its later significance, not that it achieved its intended purpose in the 1890s.

options: (A) The claim is supported because the Act's passage shows Congress was now regulating business aggressively, which means the era of noninterference had ended
(B) The claim is weakened because the Act's earliest major courtroom uses targeted labor unions, as in the 1894 injunction against the Pullman strike.
(C) The claim is weakened because the great merger wave of 1895-1904 came after the Act, which shows the law caused even more consolidation
(D) The claim is supported because modern antitrust law descends from the Sherman Act, which proves it worked as intended from the start
items.stem: Congress passed the Sherman Antitrust Act in 1890 to restrain monopolistic business combinations. Which of the following best evaluates the claim that the Act achieved its intended purpose during the 1890s?

items.explanation: Carnegie was one of the richest steelmakers in the world, and his essay is a defense of why men like him should keep their fortunes -- he had a direct interest in making great wealth look natural and good. That point of view shapes everything he says, so the essay tells us how industrialists justified their wealth, not what mill life was actually like for workers. A writer's claim about workers is not evidence of workers' views, his wealth does not make him reliable on their experience, and his call for giving does not show he shared modern values.
items.fact_source: Andrew Carnegie, 'The Gospel of Wealth,' North American Review (1889); Gilded Age labor conflict - Great Railroad Strike (1877), Haymarket (1886).

option_explanations.A: Wrong. This takes Carnegie's own claim -- that inequality was 'inevitable' -- as proof of what workers thought. A writer's assertion about workers is not evidence of workers' views, especially when the writer benefits from that assertion.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Wealth and success do not make a source reliable about workers' experiences; Carnegie's position as an owner is exactly what limits the essay's use as evidence about mill life.
option_explanations.C: Right. A steel magnate defending industrial fortunes writes from the owner's side; his purpose is to justify wealth, which limits what the essay can show about workers' daily experiences.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. This projects modern ideas of corporate responsibility onto 1889; Carnegie's call for philanthropy served his defense of great fortunes, not a modern concern for workers.

options: (A) Because Carnegie openly acknowledged that inequality was inevitable, the essay shows that most workers accepted dangerous conditions as the price of progress
(B) Because Carnegie was one of the richest and most successful industrialists, his account of industrial life is the most reliable one available
(C) Carnegie's position as a steel magnate means the essay defends industrial fortunes, so it cannot substitute for evidence about workers' mill life.
(D) Carnegie's call for the wealthy to give back shows he shared modern ideas of corporate responsibility, so the essay proves industrialists cared about workers
items.stem: Which of the following best evaluates the limits of using this essay as evidence about the experiences of steelworkers in the 1880s?

stimulus.text: In his 1889 essay 'The Gospel of Wealth,' steel magnate Andrew Carnegie argued that great fortunes were a natural and necessary product of civilization's progress, and that the wealthy should treat themselves as trustees bound to spend their surplus for the community's welfare.

items.explanation: The Dawes Act fits a continuous federal push after the Civil War to transfer western land from Native nations to railroads, miners, and settlers -- the same campaign behind the transcontinental railroad land grants and the reservation wars of the 1870s. Allotment broke up tribal landholding so 'surplus' acres could be sold to non-Natives. It was not a treaty negotiation, it did not recognize changes Native families had made, and it is not explained by the reformers' own stated rationale.
items.fact_source: Dawes Severalty Act (1887); Congress ended treaty-making with tribes (1871); Ghost Dance movement and Wounded Knee (1890); federal railroad land grants and post-Civil War western land policy.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The Dawes Act imposed allotment unilaterally; Congress had ended treaty-making with tribes in 1871. This option projects an earlier pattern onto a later policy that broke with it.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Some Native families farmed individually, but allotment was imposed on all tribal nations whether they farmed or not -- and the law's point was to declare most of the land 'surplus' and sell it. A change some families made cannot explain a policy forced on everyone.
option_explanations.C: Right. After the Civil War the federal government systematically worked to open the West to railroads, mining, and white settlement; the Dawes Act served that campaign by dissolving communal Native landholding and selling off the 'surplus.'
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The reformers' stated hope of 'civilizing' Native Americans through property was their justification for the policy, not the engine behind it -- the engine was transferring land to non-Native hands.

options: (A) It continued the established federal practice of acquiring Native land through treaties negotiated with tribal leaders
(B) Many Native families were already farming individually by the 1880s, so allotment merely recognized a change Native Americans had already made for themselves
(C) It extended the post-Civil War federal campaign to open the West to railroads, mining, and settlers by breaking up tribal landholding
(D) It was mainly an effort to help Native families build wealth like white homesteaders, as the law's supporters said when they promised allotment would 'civilize' Native Americans
items.stem: The Dawes Act of 1887 divided communally held tribal lands into individual allotments for Native American families, with the remaining 'surplus' land sold to non-Native settlers. Which of the following developments best explains why the Dawes Act took the form it did?

stimulus.text:
The contrast between the palace of the millionaire and the cottage of the laborer with us to-day measures the change which has come with civilization. This change, however, is not to be deplored, but welcomed as highly beneficial.

-- Andrew Carnegie, "Wealth," North American Review, 1889 (public domain)

items.stem: Which of the following best evaluates how a historian studying labor relations in the 1890s could use this passage?
options: (A) The passage is reliable evidence that factory workers' wages rose steadily, since Carnegie accurately measured the change industrial civilization had brought to workers' daily lives.

(B) The passage is best used as evidence of how leading industrialists justified inequality; because Carnegie was one of the nation's largest employers, his claims about laborers' experience need corroboration from worker sources.

(C) The passage proves that factory workers benefited from industrialization, which means the era's labor unrest was largely unnecessary and the American Federation of Labor's organizing drives addressed no genuine grievance at all.
(D) Because Carnegie personally profited from the system he defends, nothing in the passage can be trusted, so historians of the 1890s should simply not use it at all.
items.explanation: Carnegie writes as an employer defending the system that made him rich, so historians use this passage to study how industrialists justified inequality, not to learn what factory workers actually earned or felt. A self-serving source can still be valuable; what matters is matching the source to the question it can actually answer and checking its claims against other evidence.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. It takes Carnegie's argument as neutral fact. A justification written by one of the era's largest employers is not wage data, and accepting its claims about workers' lives repeats the source's own self-defense as if it were measurement.
option_explanations.B: Right. It names both the correct use (evidence of how industrialists justified inequality) and the limit (Carnegie's position as a major employer means his claims about workers need worker-source corroboration).
option_explanations.C: Wrong. It treats one man's defense of the system as proof of how workers actually fared, then uses that overgeneralization to erase the very grievances that produced the era's strikes and organizing.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. It makes the opposite error: declaring a biased source useless. Historians do not throw out self-interested sources; they analyze them for what they reveal about the author's purpose and position.

items.fact_source: Verbatim excerpt from Andrew Carnegie, "Wealth," North American Review, June 1889 (public domain). Basis: Carnegie led Carnegie Steel, a dominant 1890s steel firm; the essay (the "Gospel of Wealth") argues inequality is beneficial. Historians use it as evidence of industrialists' ideology, corroborating claims about workers' conditions against labor sources.

items.stem: A student claims that the federal government's commitment to laissez-faire economics during the Gilded Age meant it took no actions that benefited businesses. Which of the following best evaluates this claim?
options: (A) The claim is valid: the Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890 shows the federal government took on big business rather than aiding it, confirming that Washington stayed neutral or hostile toward corporate growth.

(B) The claim is valid: the Constitution barred the federal government from spending public money to aid private enterprise at any point before the Progressive Era, so whatever help firms received in these years had to come entirely from state and local governments.

(C) The claim is invalid: the government granted millions of acres to railroads, kept high protective tariffs shielding manufacturers, and used federal troops and court injunctions to break strikes such as the Pullman strike of 1894.
(D) The claim is invalid: laissez-faire economics directly caused the Great Depression, which proves that federal policy consistently damaged rather than helped American businesses.
items.explanation: Laissez-faire in the Gilded Age meant the government refused to regulate business, not that it stood aside. Federal land grants to railroads, high protective tariffs for manufacturers, and troops and injunctions against strikers all actively helped business. The claim is wrong, and neither the Sherman Act on paper nor the Constitution kept Washington from acting on business's behalf.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. It confuses a law on the books with enforcement: the Sherman Act was barely used against trusts in its first decade and was instead used against labor, as in the 1894 Pullman strike. Passing a statute did not make the government neutral.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Nothing in the Constitution prohibited federal aid to business, and no such aid ban existed; the railroad land grants and tariff protection of the period were federal actions.
option_explanations.C: Right. It refutes the claim with three concrete federal actions -- railroad land grants, protective tariffs, and the use of troops and injunctions against strikers -- each of which benefited business interests.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The Great Depression began in 1929, decades after the Gilded Age ended, so it cannot directly prove anything about 1880s policy. It also gets the direction of federal help backwards.

items.fact_source: Basis: Pacific Railway Acts and Morrill Act granted tens of millions of acres of federal land to railroads; protective tariffs remained high throughout the Gilded Age (e.g., McKinley Tariff, 1890); federal troops and court injunctions suppressed strikes including the Pullman strike of 1894 (In re Debs, 1895); the Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890 was weak against trusts and used more often against unions in its early years.
